notes:
1. Industrial Growth — Meaning and Importance

  • Industrial growth refers to expansion of manufacturing, construction, mining, electricity and other industrial activities.
  • Industrialisation raises value addition by transforming raw materials and intermediate inputs into higher-value products.
  • It can improve productivity, create employment, support urbanisation, increase exports, promote technology and strengthen capital formation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Industrial Growth → Value Addition + Productivity + Employment + Exports + Technology

2. Industrial Linkages — Backward and Forward

Backward linkage:

  • An industry creates demand for inputs supplied by another sector.
  • Example → Steel industry creates demand for coal and iron ore.

Forward linkage:

  • The output of one industry becomes an input for another industry.
  • Steel supplies automobiles, machinery, construction, railways and infrastructure.
📌 Must-Memorise

Backward Linkage → Demand for Inputs

Forward Linkage → Output Becomes Another Industry's Input

3. Industrial India at Independence

  • India's modern industrial base was relatively limited at Independence.
  • Important industries included textiles, jute, iron and steel, mining and consumer-goods industries.
  • India lacked adequate capacity in capital goods, heavy engineering, machinery, electricity and industrial infrastructure.

4. Post-Independence Industrial Strategy

The early industrial strategy emphasised:

  • Heavy industry.
  • Public-sector investment.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Domestic machinery production.
  • Industrial self-reliance.
  • Import substitution.

5. Import Substitution and Self-Reliance

  • Import substitution means replacing imported industrial products with domestically produced alternatives.
  • Domestic machinery and capital-goods capability were considered essential for reducing external dependence.
📌 Must-Memorise

Import Substitution → Domestic Production Instead of Imports

6. Industrial Policy Resolution — 1948

  • The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1948 was the first major industrial-policy statement of independent India.
  • It accepted a mixed-economy framework.
  • Both public and private sectors were given roles, while strategic industries remained under stronger State control.
📌 Must-Memorise

1948 Industrial Policy → Mixed Economy

7. Industrial Policy Resolution — 1956

  • The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 became a major foundation of India's planned industrial strategy.
  • It gave a leading role to the public sector.
  • Heavy industry, regional balance, small-scale industries and prevention of excessive concentration of economic power were important objectives.
  • It was closely connected with the Second Five-Year Plan.
📌 Must-Memorise

1956 → Public Sector + Heavy Industry

Second Five-Year Plan → Heavy Industrialisation

8. Schedule A, B and C — 1956 Policy

  • Schedule A → Industries intended to be the exclusive responsibility of the State.
  • Schedule B → Industries where the State would progressively expand while private participation could continue.
  • Schedule C → Industries mainly left to the private sector, subject to regulation and licensing.
📌 Must-Memorise

A → State Exclusive

B → State Expands + Private Participation

C → Mainly Private

9. Heavy Industry — Meaning and Role

  • Heavy industries produce machinery, steel, equipment and other capital goods needed for long-term industrial development.
  • They generally require large capital investment and have long gestation periods.
  • Developing heavy industry was considered essential for industrial self-reliance.

10. Public Sector — Strategic Industrial Role

Public-sector investment played a major role in:

  • Steel.
  • Heavy engineering.
  • Power.
  • Coal.
  • Petroleum.
  • Machine tools.
  • Transport equipment.

11. Major Public-Sector Steel Plants

  • Bhilai Steel Plant → Soviet assistance.
  • Rourkela Steel Plant → West German assistance.
  • Durgapur Steel Plant → British assistance.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bhilai → Soviet Union

Rourkela → West Germany

Durgapur → United Kingdom

12. Industrial Licensing — Licence Raj

  • Industrial licensing required Government approval for major private industrial decisions.
  • Firms could require permission to establish factories, expand capacity or enter particular industries.
  • The extensive control system became commonly known as the Licence Raj.
📌 Must-Memorise

Licence Raj → Extensive Industrial Licensing

13. Objectives of Industrial Licensing

Licensing sought to:

  • Direct scarce resources.
  • Prevent excessive concentration of economic power.
  • Promote regional balance.
  • Coordinate industrial investment.
  • Support planned-development priorities.

14. Problems of the Licence Raj

Extensive licensing could cause:

  • Investment delays.
  • Entry barriers.
  • Lower competition.
  • Administrative discretion.
  • Restrictions on efficient capacity expansion.
  • Weak innovation incentives.
  • Lower productivity incentives.

15. New Industrial Policy — 1991

  • The New Industrial Policy was introduced in 1991.
  • It marked a major shift from extensive State controls towards markets, competition and private enterprise.
  • It formed part of the wider economic reforms of 1991.
📌 Must-Memorise

New Industrial Policy → 1991

16. Major Industrial Reforms of 1991

Important reforms included:

  • Industrial licensing abolished for most industries.
  • Public-sector reservation reduced.
  • Private-sector participation increased.
  • Foreign-investment rules liberalised.
  • Restrictions on expansion of large firms reduced.
  • Public-sector reform encouraged.
  • Disinvestment promoted.
  • Competition increased.
  • Technological modernisation became easier.
📌 Must-Memorise

1991 → Licensing Abolished for Most Industries

17. Pre-1991 vs Post-1991 Industrial Framework

Pre-1991:

  • Extensive licensing.
  • Stronger State controls.
  • Wider public-sector reservation.
  • More restricted foreign investment.

Post-1991:

  • Greater investment freedom.
  • More competition.
  • Greater private participation.
  • Liberalised foreign investment.
  • Increased global integration.

18. Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation

Liberalisation:

  • Reduction of unnecessary Government controls.

Privatisation:

  • Greater private ownership or participation.

Globalisation:

  • Greater integration with global trade, investment, technology and production networks.
📌 Must-Memorise

Liberalisation → Fewer Controls

Privatisation → Greater Private Role

Globalisation → World Integration

19. Privatisation and Disinvestment

  • Disinvestment can increase private participation in public enterprises.
  • Privatisation does not necessarily mean complete sale of every public-sector enterprise.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Privatisation ≠ Always 100% Sale

20. Globalisation — Industrial Effects

Globalisation gave firms greater access to:

  • Foreign capital.
  • Imported technology.
  • Export markets.
  • International production networks.

It also increased exposure to:

  • Global competition.
  • International economic shocks.

21. Manufacturing — Structural Role

  • Manufacturing converts raw materials and intermediate inputs into finished or semi-finished products.
  • It creates value addition, employment, exports and supply-chain development.
  • It also generates demand for transport, banking, insurance, logistics, engineering and business services.

22. Labour-Intensive Manufacturing

  • Labour-intensive industries use relatively more labour for a given amount of capital.
  • They are especially important in a labour-abundant economy.

Important examples include:

  • Garments.
  • Textiles.
  • Leather products.
  • Food processing.
  • Furniture.
📌 Must-Memorise

Labour-Intensive Manufacturing → Strong Employment Potential

23. Capital-Intensive Manufacturing

  • Capital-intensive industries use relatively more machinery and capital.

Examples include:

  • Steel.
  • Petrochemicals.
  • Heavy machinery.
  • Highly automated manufacturing.
  • They can improve scale, technology and productivity but may generate fewer jobs per unit of output.

24. Employment-Rich Industrialisation

  • Industrial policy must balance productivity growth with adequate job creation.
  • Higher industrial output does not automatically mean proportionately higher employment.
📌 Must-Memorise

Industrial Development → Productivity + Jobs

25. MSMEs — Meaning and Importance

  • MSME stands for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprise.
  • MSMEs operate in both manufacturing and services.

They contribute to:

  • Employment.
  • Exports.
  • Entrepreneurship.
  • Local development.
  • Supply chains.
  • Regional industrialisation.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

MSMEs ≠ Manufacturing Only

26. MSME Constraints

Major constraints include:

  • Limited affordable credit.
  • Delayed payments.
  • Technology gaps.
  • High logistics costs.
  • Weak market access.
  • Skill shortages.
  • Compliance costs.

27. MSME Competitiveness

MSME competitiveness can improve through:

  • Better credit.
  • Technology upgrading.
  • Digitalisation.
  • Lower logistics costs.
  • Skilled labour.
  • Market access.

28. Iron and Steel — Basic Industry

  • Iron and steel is a basic industry because its products are inputs for many other industries.

Steel supports:

  • Construction.
  • Automobiles.
  • Machinery.
  • Railways.
  • Infrastructure.
📌 Must-Memorise

Steel → Basic Industry

29. Textile Industry

  • Textiles are among India's oldest modern industries.

Major activities include:

  • Cotton textiles.
  • Synthetic textiles.
  • Spinning.
  • Weaving.
  • Processing.
  • Garments.
  • Garment manufacturing is especially important for employment and exports.

30. Automobile Industry

India's automobile industry includes:

  • Passenger vehicles.
  • Commercial vehicles.
  • Two-wheelers.
  • Tractors.
  • Auto components.
  • It creates strong linkages with engineering, components, logistics and transport services.

31. Pharmaceutical Industry

The pharmaceutical sector produces:

  • Generic medicines.
  • Vaccines.
  • Bulk drugs.
  • Other pharmaceutical products.

Its competitiveness depends on:

  • Scientific research.
  • Quality systems.
  • Regulation.
  • Chemistry.
  • Technology.
  • Manufacturing capability.

32. Chemicals and Petrochemicals

Chemical and petrochemical industries supply inputs to:

  • Agriculture.
  • Pharmaceuticals.
  • Textiles.
  • Plastics.
  • Other manufacturing activities.

33. Cement Industry

  • Cement is a major input for housing and infrastructure.
  • Road construction and urbanisation significantly increase demand for cement and construction materials.

34. Electronics Manufacturing

Electronics manufacturing includes:

  • Consumer electronics.
  • Communication equipment.
  • Components.
  • Advanced electronic systems.
  • Modern industries increasingly depend on electronic and digital components.

35. Food Processing

  • Food processing directly connects agriculture with industrial value addition.
  • It can increase shelf life, reduce losses and raise the market value of agricultural produce.
📌 Must-Memorise

Food Processing → Agriculture + Industry

36. Industrial Cluster — Meaning

  • An industrial cluster is a geographical concentration of interconnected firms, suppliers, workers and supporting institutions.

Benefits include:

  • Lower transaction costs.
  • Specialised labour.
  • Supplier networks.
  • Knowledge sharing.
  • Technology diffusion.
  • Better market access.
📌 Must-Memorise

Industrial Cluster → Concentration of Related Firms

37. Industrial Corridor — Meaning

  • An industrial corridor is a large development region organised around transport and infrastructure networks.

It can combine:

  • Highways.
  • Railways.
  • Industrial parks.
  • Logistics hubs.
  • Urban centres.
  • Ports.
📌 Must-Memorise

Industrial Corridor → Large Integrated Industrial Region

38. Special Economic Zone — SEZ

  • SEZ stands for Special Economic Zone.
  • It is a designated area operating under a special regulatory and trade framework intended to promote investment and exports.
  • India enacted the Special Economic Zones Act in 2005.
📌 Must-Memorise

SEZ → Special Economic Zone

SEZ Act → 2005

39. Cluster vs Corridor vs SEZ

  • Cluster → Concentration of interconnected firms.
  • Corridor → Large industrial-infrastructure region.
  • SEZ → Specially designated regulatory and trade zone.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Cluster ≠ Corridor ≠ SEZ

40. Foreign Direct Investment — FDI

  • FDI stands for Foreign Direct Investment.
  • It generally involves foreign investment establishing a lasting interest or significant influence in a domestic enterprise.

FDI can bring:

  • Capital.
  • Technology.
  • Managerial expertise.
  • Global-market access.
  • Supply-chain integration.

41. Technology Transfer

  • Technology transfer means movement of knowledge, machinery, processes, patents or technical expertise between firms or countries.
  • It can improve productivity and product quality.

42. Foreign Technology and Domestic Capability

  • Excessive dependence on imported technology can create strategic vulnerability.
  • Industrial policy therefore seeks to combine foreign investment with development of domestic technological capability.

43. FDI vs FPI

  • FDI → Longer-term strategic participation in enterprise.
  • FPI → Investment mainly in financial securities.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

FDI ≠ FPI

44. Industrial Infrastructure

Industrial growth depends on:

  • Reliable electricity.
  • Roads.
  • Railways.
  • Ports.
  • Airports.
  • Water.
  • Digital networks.
  • Warehousing.
  • Weak infrastructure raises production costs.
  • Efficient infrastructure improves competitiveness.

45. Logistics — Industrial Importance

Logistics includes:

  • Movement of goods.
  • Storage.
  • Inventory management.
  • Road freight.
  • Rail freight.
  • Ports.
  • Warehousing.
  • Cold chains.
  • Digital tracking.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lower Logistics Cost → Higher Industrial Competitiveness

46. Power Supply and Industry

  • Reliable electricity allows factories to use installed capacity effectively.
  • Power shortages can reduce capacity utilisation and raise production costs.
  • Renewable energy is increasingly important alongside conventional sources.

47. Direct and Indirect Industrial Employment

Direct employment:

  • Workers employed within factories and industrial establishments.

Indirect employment:

  • Jobs generated through supply chains and supporting services.

48. Industrialisation — Wider Employment Effects

Industrial growth creates employment in:

  • Transport.
  • Logistics.
  • Maintenance.
  • Construction.
  • Retail.
  • Accounting.
  • Finance.
  • IT.
  • Business services.

49. Regional Industrial Development

Industrial development can reduce regional disparities when industries expand beyond already-developed metropolitan centres.

Less-developed regions require:

  • Infrastructure.
  • Connectivity.
  • Supportive institutions.
  • Effective administration.

50. Industrial Location — Major Factors

Industrial location depends on:

  • Raw materials.
  • Power.
  • Labour.
  • Transport.
  • Water.
  • Markets.
  • Ports.
  • Government policy.
  • Infrastructure.

51. Raw Materials and Port Connectivity

  • Mineral-based industries may locate closer to raw-material sources.
  • Export-oriented industries may prefer locations with strong port and logistics connectivity.

52. Tamil Nadu — Major Industrial State

  • Tamil Nadu is one of India's major industrial States.
  • It has a highly diversified industrial structure.

Important sectors include:

  • Automobiles.
  • Textiles.
  • Leather.
  • Engineering.
  • Electronics.
  • Chemicals.
  • Cement.
  • Food processing.

53. Chennai — Automobile Hub

  • Chennai and surrounding districts form an important automobile-manufacturing region.
  • The ecosystem includes vehicle manufacturers, component firms, engineering companies, logistics providers and skilled technical workers.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chennai → Automobiles

54. Tamil Nadu — Electronics Ecosystem

  • Electronics and electronic-component manufacturing have expanded around Chennai and other industrial regions.

55. Coimbatore — Textile and Engineering Centre

Coimbatore is strongly associated with:

  • Textiles.
  • Spinning.
  • Textile machinery.
  • Engineering.
  • Pumps.
  • Motors.
  • Machinery.
  • Foundries.
📌 Must-Memorise

Coimbatore → Textiles + Engineering + Pumps

56. Tiruppur — Knitwear

  • Tiruppur is especially known for knitwear production and exports.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tiruppur → Knitwear

57. Erode and Karur — Textile Centres

  • Erode and surrounding areas are important textile centres.
  • Karur is also an important textile and garment-related centre.

58. Ranipet, Ambur and Vellore — Leather

  • Ranipet has an important leather and footwear cluster.
  • Ambur is strongly associated with leather and footwear.
  • Vellore and surrounding areas also have significant leather-related activity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ranipet–Ambur → Leather and Footwear

59. Tamil Nadu — Cement Industry

  • Tamil Nadu has significant cement production.
  • Limestone resources and industrial infrastructure support the industry.

60. Sivakasi — Industrial Specialisation

Sivakasi is historically associated with:

  • Fireworks.
  • Match production.
  • Printing.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sivakasi → Fireworks + Matches + Printing

61. SIPCOT

  • SIPCOT is associated primarily with development of major industrial complexes, parks and large industrial infrastructure.
📌 Must-Memorise

SIPCOT → Major Industrial Parks and Infrastructure

62. SIDCO

  • SIDCO is associated particularly with development and support of small industries and industrial estates.
📌 Must-Memorise

SIDCO → Small Industries

63. SIPCOT vs SIDCO

  • SIPCOT → Larger industrial complexes and parks.
  • SIDCO → Small industries and industrial estates.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

SIPCOT ≠ SIDCO

64. Tamil Nadu Industrial Cluster Memory Chain

  • Chennai → Automobiles.
  • Coimbatore → Textiles + Engineering + Pumps.
  • Tiruppur → Knitwear.
  • Erode / Karur → Textiles.
  • Ranipet / Ambur / Vellore → Leather.
  • Sivakasi → Fireworks + Matches + Printing.

65. Industrial Growth — Infrastructure and Skill Challenges

Major constraints include:

  • Infrastructure gaps.
  • Skill shortages.
  • Technical workforce gaps.
  • Affordable-credit constraints.
  • High logistics costs.
  • Need for technological upgrading.

66. Global Competition and Import Dependence

  • International competition requires improvements in productivity, quality, technology and cost efficiency.
  • Dependence on imported components, machinery, energy or strategic raw materials can create vulnerabilities.

67. Industrialisation — Environmental Costs

Industrial activity can contribute to:

  • Air pollution.
  • Water pollution.
  • Hazardous waste.
  • Greenhouse-gas emissions.
  • Natural-resource depletion.

68. Regional Concentration of Industry

  • Industrial development can become concentrated in a limited number of States and metropolitan regions.
  • Balanced industrialisation therefore requires wider infrastructure and investment distribution.

69. Automation — Employment Challenge

  • Highly automated factories can raise production without proportionately increasing employment.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Higher Industrial Output ≠ Automatically More Jobs

70. Industrial Strategy — Technology and Employment

India needs both:

  • Technologically advanced industries.
  • Employment-intensive manufacturing.
📌 Must-Memorise

Industrial Strategy → Technology + Employment

71. Green Industrialisation

  • Green industrialisation seeks to combine industrial growth with lower environmental impact.

Important approaches include:

  • Renewable energy.
  • Energy efficiency.
  • Electric mobility.
  • Recycling.
  • Low-carbon manufacturing.

72. Circular Economy

  • A circular economy seeks to reuse, repair, recycle and recover materials instead of relying only on a produce-use-discard model.
📌 Must-Memorise

Circular Economy → Reuse + Repair + Recycle + Recover

73. Future Industrial Policy — Core Priorities

Future industrial policy must balance:

  • Growth.
  • Employment.
  • Competitiveness.
  • Technology.
  • Domestic capability.
  • Sustainability.

📌 Must-Memorise
  • 1948 → First Industrial Policy Resolution.
  • 1956 → Public-sector + heavy-industry emphasis.
  • 1991 → New Industrial Policy + liberalisation.
  • 2005 → SEZ Act.

83. TNPSC Traps

  • Industrialisation is broader than manufacturing alone.
  • Manufacturing belongs to the secondary sector.
  • Backward linkage means demand for inputs.
  • Forward linkage means output becomes another industry's input.
  • Industrial Policy Resolution 1948 and 1956 are different.
  • 1948 → Mixed economy.
  • 1956 → Public-sector leadership and heavy industry.
  • 1956 policy was closely associated with the Second Five-Year Plan.
  • Schedule A → State exclusive.
  • Schedule B → Progressive State role with private participation.
  • Schedule C → Mainly private sector.
  • Bhilai → Soviet assistance.
  • Rourkela → West German assistance.
  • Durgapur → British assistance.
  • Licence Raj means extensive licensing and regulation.
  • New Industrial Policy → 1991.
  • Industrial licensing was abolished for most industries in 1991.
  • Liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation are different.
  • Privatisation does not always mean complete sale.
  • Labour-intensive and capital-intensive industries are different.
  • MSMEs operate in manufacturing and services.
  • Steel is a basic industry.
  • Food processing links agriculture and industry.
  • Cluster, corridor and SEZ are different.
  • SEZ Act → 2005.
  • FDI and FPI are different.
  • FDI can bring capital, technology and management.
  • Industrial location depends on raw materials, power, labour, transport, water, markets, ports and policy.
  • Higher industrial output does not automatically create proportionately more jobs.
  • Tamil Nadu has a diversified industrial base.
  • Chennai → Automobiles.
  • Coimbatore → Textiles, engineering and pumps.
  • Tiruppur → Knitwear.
  • Ranipet–Ambur → Leather and footwear.
  • Sivakasi → Fireworks, matches and printing.
  • SIPCOT and SIDCO are different.
  • SIPCOT → Larger industrial parks.
  • SIDCO → Small industries.
  • Industrialisation can create environmental costs.
  • Green industrialisation combines growth with sustainability.
